runs.u: Can you recommend a messaging app?
runs.reply:
There’s no single “best” messaging app—it really depends on what you prioritize. Here are some solid options based on different needs:

**For strong privacy and security**
- **Signal**: Open source, end-to-end encryption by default for all messages, voice/video calls, and even stickers. Minimal metadata collection. Recommended by security experts and used by journalists. Your contacts need Signal too to get the full encryption, but it works seamlessly once set up.
- **Session** (if you want even more anonymity): Decentralized, no phone number required, uses onion routing. Less mainstream but very private.

**For a good balance of features, privacy, and wide adoption**
- **Telegram**: Cloud-based, feature-rich (large groups, channels, bots, file sharing up to 2GB), and has optional end-to-end encryption in “Secret Chats.” Default chats are encrypted server-client but stored on servers (so you can access from multiple devices). Great for communities and power users, but if you want every conversation truly E2EE by default, Signal might be better.
- **WhatsApp**: Uses the Signal protocol for end-to-end encryption by default. Extremely popular globally, so almost everyone you know is likely on it. Owned by Meta, which raises some concerns about metadata sharing with Facebook (though message content is encrypted). Convenient if you just need to chat with existing contacts.

**For Apple users**
- **iMessage**: Seamless integration across Apple devices, end-to-end encrypted, supports rich media and effects. Excellent if you and your contacts are all in the Apple ecosystem, but falls back to SMS/MMS for Android users (unencrypted, green bubbles).

**For simplicity and cross-platform basics**
- **Google Messages** (with RCS enabled): If you’re on Android, it’s the default SMS app with RCS chat features (typing indicators, read receipts, better media) when chatting with other RCS users. Google's RCS is encrypted in transit, but it's less battle-tested than Signal. Good if you want a default app that works with phone numbers without adding a new service.

**Bottom line**:  
- Go with **Signal** if privacy is your top concern and you can get friends/family to switch.  
- Use **Telegram** if you want powerful group/channel features and don’t mind the hybrid encryption model.  
- Stick with **WhatsApp** if you need maximum compatibility and convenience.  

If you tell me a bit more about what you need (groups, file sharing, privacy level, operating system), I can narrow it down further.

### Top contenders at a glance

| App | Strongest points | Watch out for |
|-----|------------------|---------------|
| **Signal** | Gold standard for privacy and security. Open source, end‑to‑end encrypted by default, collects virtually no metadata. Great voice/video calls. | Smaller user base – you may need to persuade others to install it. |
| **WhatsApp** | Huge global user base. End‑to‑end encryption (by default) for texts and calls. Simple and reliable. | Owned by Meta (Facebook). Collects metadata (contacts, usage patterns), and privacy policies have raised concerns. |
| **Telegram** | Packed with features: large groups, channels, bots, custom stickers, file sharing up to 2 GB. Fast and cloud‑based. | Only “Secret Chats” are end‑to‑end encrypted. Regular chats and group chats use server‑side encryption (Telegram holds the keys). Not truly private in default mode. |
| **iMessage** (Apple) | Seamless for Apple users, end‑to‑end encrypted, tightly integrated. Falls back to SMS for non‑Apple contacts. | Apple‑only; mixed‑platform groups can be messy, SMS fallback is not secure. |
| **Messenger** (Facebook) | Many people already use it; built into Facebook. | No longer default end‑to‑end encryption (you must opt into “Secret Conversations”). Heavy data collection by Meta. |
| **Discord** | Great for communities, gaming, and voice hangouts. | Not built primarily for private 1‑on‑1 messaging; no end‑to‑end encryption. |
| **Slack / Teams** | Work and team collaboration. | Overkill for personal use, not designed as a simple chat app. |

### Quick recommendations based on your priorities

- **If privacy and security are your #1 concern:**  
  → **Signal**. It’s as private as modern messaging gets, and the user experience is pleasant and simple.

- **If you need the largest audience and easiest adoption (everyone already has it):**  
  → **WhatsApp**. It’s the path of least resistance, though you trade some privacy for that convenience.

- **If you want tons of features (channels, bots, huge groups, cloud sync):**  
  → **Telegram**. Just remember to start a Secret Chat when you really need end‑to‑end encryption.

- **If you and your contacts all live in the Apple ecosystem:**  
  → Stick with **iMessage** for personal chats; it’s secure and effortless.

- **If you want a single app that covers both private chats and community hangouts (and you don’t mind weaker encryption):**  
  → **Telegram** or **Discord**, depending on your vibe (Telegram is more like a messaging app, Discord is more like a chat‑with‑servers app).

If you tell me a bit more about your situation—who you’ll be messaging with, what features you need, and how much privacy matters—I can give you a more focused pick.

runs.u: Can you recommend a messaging app?
runs.reply:
Choosing a messaging app really depends on what you value most—privacy, features, platform support, or how many of your friends are already on it. Here’s a breakdown of the top options as of 2025:

### 🥇 Signal – Best for Privacy & Security
- **Why:** Open-source, end-to-end encryption by default for all chats and calls. Minimal metadata collection. Gold standard for privacy-conscious users.
- **Get it if:** You want the most secure experience, don’t mind fewer bells and whistles, and can convince your contacts to switch.

### 🥈 WhatsApp – Best for Reach & Reliability
- **Why:** Over 2 billion users, so your contacts are almost certainly there. Full end-to-end encryption (Signal protocol), voice/video calls, stories, communities.
- **Caveat:** Owned by Meta, which shares metadata (who you talk to, when, device info) for ad targeting. The app itself is secure, but the parent company’s data practices are a concern for some.

### 🥉 Telegram – Best for Features & Flexibility
- **Why:** Cloud-based, massive group limits (200,000+), channels, bots, custom themes, large file sharing (2 GB+). Secret Chats offer end-to-end encryption, but **default chats do not**.
- **Get it if:** You want a full-featured, multi-device experience without relying on your phone all the time. Just be aware that standard one-on-one and group chats are stored on Telegram’s servers and can be accessed by authorities with legal requests.

### Other strong contenders:
- **iMessage** – Best for Apple-only groups. End-to-end encrypted, seamless integration. Falls back to SMS with non-Apple users.
- **Threema** – Swiss-based, fully anonymous (no phone number required). Paid app, very strong privacy.
- **Session** – Decentralized, onion-routed, no phone number required. Minimal metadata, but slightly slower and niche.
- **Matrix / Element** – Open protocol, self-hosting option. Great for communities or organizations wanting full control over their data.

### Quick summary:
| If your priority is… | Go with… |
|----------------------|----------|
| Absolute privacy & minimal data collection | **Signal** |
| Talking to the most people right now | **WhatsApp** |
| Power-user features, bots, and cloud sync | **Telegram** (use Secret Chats for sensitive stuff) |
| Apple ecosystem only | **iMessage** |

**My personal recommendation:** Start with **Signal** for private conversations and ask your closest circles to join you there. Keep **WhatsApp** as the fallback for everyone else, and use **Telegram** if you love its channels and tools.

Want a more specific recommendation based on your use case (work, family, activism, etc.)? Let me know!

- **Global reach with local roots**: AP has reporters in about 250 locations worldwide, so you get strong international coverage alongside U.S. news.
- **Transparent corrections**: They have a clear, prominent corrections policy and don’t bury mistakes.

The downside is that AP is mostly straight reporting — you won’t find much long-form analysis or strong narrative voice. So for deeper understanding, I’d still pair it with something like *The Economist* or *The Atlantic* a few times a week. But if you can only have one daily news habit, AP keeps you reliably informed with minimal noise.
